title: The powers are obstacles to samadhi (3.37)
word: The powers are obstacles to sama
hook: in the middle of the list of powers, one sutra turns the whole list over: seen from samadhi, these are obstacles

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heart, the lotus-house where samyama comes to know the mind. Did you decide one thing from your chest instead of your head? Day four hundred seventy-three.

A swimmer wins gold. On the podium, the medal shines against her chest, heavy and real, and the whole stadium stands. Now imagine she wore it in the next race. The same gold that honored her on land would drag at her neck in the water. Same medal. In one place, a prize. In another, a weight. For days now Patanjali has been listing powers: past and future, other minds, strength, the stars, the body's map. Today, right in the middle of the list, he stops and tells you what the medal weighs in the water.
screen: `GOLD ON THE PODIUM.` → `THE SAME GOLD IN THE WATER.` → `A PRIZE, OR A WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Two sutras set it up. Sutra 3.35: experience happens because the mind's clearest part and the true self, the seer, aren't told apart. By samyama on the seer's own purpose, the seer is known. Sutra 3.36: from that come flashes of intuition, a finer hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell. Then sutra 3.37, short and sharp. Te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah. These are obstacles in samadhi. In the outward-turned mind, they're powers. Two words carry the weight. Upasarga means an obstacle, a trouble, something that comes at you. Siddhi is an accomplishment. Patanjali applies both to the very same things. The difference is where you stand. Vyutthana, the rising-out, is the mind turned toward the world. From there, knowing the future looks like an achievement. From inside samadhi, it's a distraction, one more thing to look at when the whole point was to stop looking at things and rest as the seer. That's the warning. Notice what Patanjali doesn't say. He doesn't call the powers fake. He doesn't call them evil. He keeps listing them for the rest of the book. He just tells you plainly what they cost if you chase them. And the old teachers took it to heart. Story after story in the tradition shows a sage who could have done something astonishing and didn't bother, because it would have pulled them back out. On an ordinary Tuesday the powers look smaller: praise, being right, a clever answer. Gold on the podium. A weight in the water.
screen: `THE SEER KNOWN; SUBTLE SENSES WAKE.` · `UPASARGA: AN OBSTACLE.` · `SIDDHI: AN ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `IT DEPENDS WHERE YOU STAND.` · then, large: `THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices the shiny things. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Sooner or later a pleasant thought will arrive: something you did well, a compliment, a clever idea. Notice how it tugs, how it wants to be looked at. You don't have to push it away. Just see it as a medal, nod to it, and let your attention slip back into the water of the breath. The bell holds the time.
The powers are obstacles to samadhi. In the outward mind they're accomplishments; in absorption, they're in the way.
screen: `THE POWERS ARE OBSTACLES TO SAMADHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the warning. Today, when you're praised or prove someone wrong, enjoy it for one breath, then take the medal off before the next swim. Day four hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 473 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ENTERING ANOTHER BODY; LEVITATION; RADIANCE.`

howItsDone: Teachers in many Hindu lineages quote sutra 3.37 to warn students against seeking powers, and stories of saints often praise those who had such abilities and set them aside for the sake of liberation or devotion.

pairs: a prize that becomes a weight

he keeps listing them; he says they are obstacles in samadhi.

the list goes on; the warning sits in the middle of it.

fork.setup: deep in practice, you suddenly sense what will happen tomorrow. what does sutra 3.37 suggest you're facing?
options: an obstacle to absorption, however impressive.
fork.reveal: 3.37: these are obstacles in samadhi; only in the outward-turned mind are they accomplishments.

original.note: Sanskrit upasarga: an obstacle, a trouble that comes upon you; in 3.37, what the powers are in samādhi.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga rewards you with powers.
what it means: seen from absorption, the powers are obstacles; they only look like achievements from the outward-turned mind.
what a scholar hears: te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah (3.37): the same items, two names, by standpoint; numbering varies (3.37 or 3.38) by edition.
